chunks: "Random access means you can read or write any location directly, and it takes about the same amount of time no matter which address you pick or which one you accessed last.
'Random' doesn't mean the data or the order is unpredictable; it means the access order is arbitrary and unconstrained, the hardware doesn't care.
It's contrasted with sequential access, like a magnetic tape: to get to the 1,000th byte you have to wind past the first 999, so the access time depends on where the head is and where the data is.
A hard drive is in between, because it has to move the head and wait for the platter to rotate. The reason RAM can do this is how it's built.
An address goes into a decoder that activates exactly one word line, and the selected cells drive the bit lines, so the time depends on the circuit, not on how far away the address is.
The same would be true of ROM or flash reads. In real systems it's only approximately true.
DRAM has row buffers, so reading another address in the same open row is faster than opening a new row, and caches make recently used addresses faster.
So software still benefits from locality, but the point is the hardware gives you direct access to any byte."
